deep.reconstruction:
Setting (inferred from this page and the next). Grothendieck is studying a system (arrangement) of pseudo-lines D_i, apparently in a projective or affine plane Y, possibly through a covering X~. The first lines warn that the images of the D_i in X~ must not be confused with the covering of the 'rives' (sides/banks) of the D_i. That covering depends on a choice of orientation of each D_i.

Item (i) sets up a model. There is a map phi: X -> Y from a surface X carrying a curve K, which cuts X into 'faces' (the faces of (X,K)). The structural conditions are:
1) phi restricted to each face is an immersion. He first wrote 'plongement' (embedding), crossed it out and replaced it with 'immersion'.
2) Near each ordinary point of K, phi is an ordinary 'folding'. The English word is used.
3) Near each vertex s of K, phi is a relative 'double folding' involving one further curve (written xi in the transcription) and the two branches of K through s.
4) L := phi^{-1}(union of the D_i). The crossed-out drafts suggest the intended statement is K ∩ L = (phi|K)^{-1}(X_1), with X_1 the union of the lines (the 1-skeleton of the arrangement).

The word 'folding' and the later 'symmetrisation law around an edge' (next page: a reflection sigma_a fixing the edge a, acting on a tubular neighbourhood T_a) indicate paper folding, not Whitney's generic fold. Locally phi looks like (x,y) -> (|x|,y) along a crease and like (x,y) -> (|x|,|y|) at a vertex. On that reading, (X,K) is a crease pattern and phi a folded-flat realisation of it.

The 'Cor.' reads: a point of K ∩ L that is not a vertex of K maps to a vertex of the arrangement. Such a point is a critical point of K: one of the two lines through phi(s) is a crease line, i.e. one of the ordinary edges of K. The marginal NB and the coloured figure illustrate this. The figure shows a green boundary curve (part of the boundary of F), red/orange pseudo-lines through s, and a grey mark for the privileged ('marked') side. The NB says it suffices that the branches of F at s, with their privileged side, all meet at one point of the boundary of F. It adds that one must take care of the 'contours' of the components of K_0.

Item (j) (transcribed 'f)'). Take a face F. At each critical point s on its boundary whose marked side (cf. (d)) is exterior to F, correct the contour by a small bulge, so that s lies on the privileged side. This gives a slightly enlarged face F' ⊃ F. The pair (F', F' ∩ L) is then an affine 'relative position', i.e. a local affine pseudo-line configuration, suitably decorated. So each face carries a well-defined affine arrangement, and the bulge rule settles the ambiguity at critical boundary points.

Item (k). An exceptional edge of K is called stable, unstable or semi-stable according to whether the two relative positions on the incident faces are both stable, both unstable, or mixed. Claim: at every exceptional vertex, the privileged side of the ordinary branch of K through it faces the unstable exceptional edge ('cont. forcé', forced contour).

The next page continues with a symmetrisation law across exceptional and ordinary edges, and with indices of edges such as n - (nu_{s0} - 1) - (nu_{s1} - 1). It also aims to reconstruct the combinatorial structure Sigma from K plus numerical data (vertex indices nu(s), edge indices nu(a)).

Aim: to encode a pseudo-line arrangement, or a family or mutation class of arrangements, by a combinatorial 'folding' datum (X, K, L, phi). Local stability or instability of the face configurations then reads off along exceptional edges.
errors: The text is a working draft with many self-corrections. 'Plongement' is replaced by 'immersion' in condition 1). Condition 4) and the corollary are rewritten several times, and the final formulation K ∩ L = (phi|K)^{-1}(X_1) is only implicit.
The marginal 'NB (pourquoi?)' shows Grothendieck himself had not yet justified why the privileged branches at a critical point all meet in one boundary point. This is a gap at this stage.
Item (k)'s claim about the forced contour at exceptional vertices is asserted without proof. Its correctness cannot be checked without the definitions in (d) and the earlier pages.
The next page records a 'correction!' of the edge-index formula, so the numerical bookkeeping was still unsettled.

ideas.what: Modelling a pseudo-line configuration through a 'folding' map phi: X -> Y from a surface with a crease curve K. Faces are immersed, edges are ordinary folds, vertices are double folds, and reflection symmetries act across edges.
ideas.modern_name: piecewise-immersive folding map / flat-folded crease pattern (origami-type map); reflection-orbifold-like local structure
ideas.usually_credited_to: Flat-foldability theory: Kawasaki, Maekawa, Justin (1980s); Robertson (1977) on isometric foldings of Riemannian manifolds
ideas.where_published: Pseudo-lines are perhaps mentioned in passing in Esquisse d'un programme (1984) (unsure); this folding model is not published

ideas.what: The preimage L = phi^{-1}(union D_i) and the characterisation of K ∩ L as preimages of the arrangement's 1-skeleton. Non-vertex points of K ∩ L are 'critical points' lying over arrangement vertices.
ideas.modern_name: pull-back of an arrangement under a folding / critical-point incidence

ideas.what: Bulging correction of a face at critical boundary points, so that each face F' carries a canonical affine pseudo-line configuration (F', F' ∩ L).
ideas.modern_name: local affine sub-arrangement / localisation of an oriented matroid at a cell
ideas.usually_credited_to: Localisation in oriented matroids: Las Vergnas, Bland (1970s)

ideas.what: Classification of exceptional edges as stable, unstable or semi-stable from the incident face configurations, and a forced-side rule at exceptional vertices.
ideas.modern_name: possibly related to mutations / triangle flips and the stability of simple arrangements; no clear modern equivalent
ideas.usually_credited_to: unsure (Ringel's flip graph of arrangements, 1956, is the nearest theme)

missed.claim: Grothendieck sets up a folding-map ('crease pattern') model of pseudo-line arrangements: surface X, crease curve K, folds and double folds, reflection symmetries across edges. He aims to reconstruct the arrangement combinatorics from K plus integer vertex and edge indices. The programme is left in draft form.
missed.quote: Au voisinage de tout point de K, φ a la structure d'un "folding" ordinaire. ... Au voisinage des sommets de K, φ a la structure d'un "double folding" relatif
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Pseudo-line arrangements (oriented matroids of rank 3, wiring diagrams, Ringel flips) and flat-foldable origami are each well developed, but they are rarely linked through a single folding-map formalism. A specialist might find this an unexplored encoding.

missed.claim: Implicit link between the combinatorics of pseudo-line systems and the local theory of folding/reflection maps of surfaces. The stability classification of exceptional edges suggests a stratification of arrangement space read off from the fold locus.
missed.quote: Appelons une arête exceptionnelle stable ou instable (ou semi-stable) suivant que les deux p.r. incidentes correspondantes
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This could bear on the topology of realisation and mutation spaces of arrangements, where the flip graph structure is studied. The text is too fragmentary to claim a concrete result.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a technical intermediate page of Grothendieck's largely unstudied 1983-84 pseudo-line project. The folding/crease-pattern formalism is unusual and seemingly unpublished, but it is fragmentary, self-corrected and without finished results, so its value is mainly historical and suggestive.
transcription_corrections: The right-column item labelled 'f)' is almost certainly 'j)'. It follows the circled 'i)' of the left column and precedes 'k)'.
'(i) On a une application [?]' is followed directly by 'X --φ--> Y'. The insertion above 'structurelles' reads something like '{quelles contractions}' and is uncertain.
The symbol read as 'ξ' in item 3 ('ξ et les deux branches de K passant en s') may be a different letter (possibly L or ζ). It is unclear in the image.
In (j), 'les options affines' is doubtful. It may read 'positions affines' or 'configurations affines', in line with 'position relative' just before.
The left-margin crossed-out notes beside items 1)-2) contain fragments like 'points critiques ... ordinaires ... points de K' and are mostly illegible.
The page number '45' appears at the bottom left.
